newsitem.title: USA: Clinton and congressional leaders meet on budget.
newsitem.headline: Clinton and congressional leaders meet on budget.

text.p: President Bill Clinton and Republican leaders of Congress pledged on Tuesday to work to pass balanced budget legislation but neither side showed signs that they were close to bridging their differences.

Clinton, who returned from Europe on Saturday, invited the congressional Republicans and their Democratic counterparts to the White House to give a push to legislation now winding its way through Congress to balance the budget by the year 2002.

He began the meeting by insisting that despite a dramatic and unexpected narrowing in the U.S. budget deficit, it was critical to pass legislation enacting the balanced budget agreement that he and congressional Republicans reached in May.

"Now that we're back here, I think that clearly the first order of business is to go on with the work of balancing the budget," he said, flanked by Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott and Speaker of the House of Representatives Newt Gingrich.

"There are some ... who've argued that since the deficit has dropped dramatically it will somehow disappear," Clinton told reporters at the start of the meeting. "I have to say that I emphatically disagree with that."

The Congressional Budget Office has concluded that the deficit will shrink to less than $50 billion this year, well below the $67 billion projection it made two months ago and a far cry from the $124 billion it forecast earlier this year.

White House officials said the meeting was designed in part to help get the balanced budget legislation passed before Congress goes on vacation in August. Several top legislators, including Lott, said they thought this was possible.

While several participants said that Tuesday's nearly one-hour meeting in the White House was constructive, none offered hard evidence that the two sides were moving closer together on the host of issues that divide them.
These include the structure of a proposed five-year, $85 billion tax cut, including how to cut the capital gains tax and how to implement a proposed $500-per-child tax credit.

The differences also include whether to raise the age at which U.S. citizens are eligible for the Medicare health care programme for the elderly and whether to "means-test" benefits, so that wealthier people would have to pay higher premiums.

There were even some disputes among the Republicans about what took place at the meeting. House Republican Leader Dick Armey told reporters there "seemed to be a general agreement" that a Senate plan to make wealthy seniors pay higher Medicare premiums should be postponed while Lott said he believed the issue was still on the table.

Other particpants in the meeting, which included Senate Minority Leader Tom Daschle and House Minority Leader Dick Gephardt, both Democrats, said it was designed not so much as a negotiating session, but an airing of views.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry agreed, and suggested that it will take time for all the issues to be hammered out. "I think they've got a ways to go," McCurry said. "Everyone seems determined to try to do it and do it quickly ... but it's going to take a lot of hard work."

House and Senate members last week began a conference to resolve differences between the budget bills passed by the two houses of Congress. Once a "reconciliation" bill is agreed, both would vote on it and send it to Clinton for signature.
"There are a lot of major issues still unresolved," House Ways and Means Committee Chairman Bill Archer, a Texas Republican, told reporters of the conference's work on taxes.
